analysis.investment_thesis: Jamna Auto is a decent-quality business with ROCE of ~21%, but at a market cap of ₹5,140 Cr against FY25 EBIT of only ₹305 Cr, the earnings yield sits at ~5.9% — just below my 6% minimum threshold, making it neither cheap enough nor growing fast enough to warrant a Magic Formula buy. The cyclical commercial vehicle exposure and FY25 revenue/profit decline further reduce near-term conviction.
key_strengths: ROIC/ROCE of ~20-29% (depending on capital base) signals a genuinely good business with competitive advantages in CV leaf springs
Near-debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.15, borrowings collapsed from ₹152 Cr in 2020 to ₹12 Cr in 2025)
Market leader in parabolic leaf springs for commercial vehicles — a niche, sticky OEM supply relationship
key_risks: Earnings yield of ~5.9% (EBIT ₹305 Cr / EV ~₹5,140 Cr) is below my 6% buy threshold — stock is not cheap enough for the Magic Formula
Highly cyclical: revenue swung from ₹2,135 Cr (FY19) → ₹1,079 Cr (FY21) → ₹2,270 Cr (FY25), with FY25 already showing a -6.5% revenue decline vs FY24 peak
FCF is erratic (negative in FY20, FY22, FY24) and CWIP surged to ₹270 Cr in FY25 — heavy capex cycle underway may suppress free cash for 2-3 years
red_flags: FY25 revenue fell ₹157 Cr (-6.5%) and net profit dropped from ₹205 Cr to ₹180 Cr — earnings are contracting, not growing
P/E of 25.4x on a cyclical auto-parts manufacturer is expensive; Magic Formula earnings yield of ~5.9% fails my 6% minimum hurdle
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Jamna Auto: Earnings Yield = EBIT/EV = ₹305 Cr / ~₹5,140 Cr ≈ 5.9% — fractionally below my 6% floor. Return on Capital using equity + debt - cash (₹1,036 Cr) gives EBIT/capital of ~29%, while the reported ROCE of 20.7% is a more conservative read. Either way, the business quality side of the formula is respectable — sustained mid-to-high-20s ROIC over several years, very low debt, and strong OEM relationships in CV leaf springs. However, the valuation side of the formula fails: at P/E 25.4x and earnings yield sub-6%, I'm paying a full price for a cyclical company in what may be a downcycle.

The FY25 data is a concern — revenue declined, EBITDA fell from ₹334 Cr to ₹311 Cr, and free cash flow is only ₹103 Cr against a ₹196 Cr capex outlay. CWIP ballooned to ₹270 Cr (vs ₹121 Cr a year ago), signalling a major expansion bet. This is not a bad business — it is a well-run, low-leverage CV components manufacturer — but it is not a Magic Formula bargain at current prices. I'd want to see earnings yield push above 8-9% (stock price ~₹85-95) before getting excited.
